question: What is the main genetic material found inside the HIV virus?
explanation: Think of HIV as an RNA virus! It carries two strands of single-stranded RNA, which it uses to make DNA once inside your body's cells. You've got this! [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: What is the main job of the gp120 surface proteins on HIV?

options.A: To replicate the viral RNA directly inside the bloodstream
options.B: To recognize and bind to receptors on target host cells
options.C: To prevent destruction by the human liver enzymes
options.D: To form the protective inner core capsid of the virus

explanation: Great job! The gp120 spikes act like a key that fits right into the CD4 receptors on immune cells, letting the virus sneak inside. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which body fluid carries the highest amount of infectious HIV?
explanation: Spot on! Blood, semen, and vaginal fluids have high viral loads capable of spreading HIV, unlike everyday touch or fluids like sweat and tears. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: Why does HIV specifically attack CD4+ T-cells and macrophages?

options.A: These cells circulate faster than other blood cells in the human body
options.B: These cells produce large amounts of viral protease that activate the virus
options.C: These cells ingest the virus to destroy it permanently before it multiplies
options.D: These cells express surface receptors and co-receptors that the virus needs to enter

explanation: You got it! HIV needs specific matching receptors (like CD4) on the cell surface to hook on and gain entry. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: Which viral enzyme helps convert the virus's RNA into DNA?
explanation: Well done! Because HIV works 'in reverse' from RNA to DNA, it relies on an enzyme called reverse transcriptase to do the trick. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: What happens right after HIV DNA successfully joins the host cell's chromosomes?

options.A: The infected cell transforms directly into a malignant tumor cell
options.B: The virus destroys all antibodies circulating in the bloodstream
options.C: The host cell immediately undergoes programmed cell death
options.D: The host cell machinery begins producing viral proteins and RNA

explanation: Exactly! Once the viral DNA sneaks into the host's DNA, the host cell is tricked into manufacturing new copies of the virus. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: During which stage of HIV do patients often get a sudden spike in virus levels and flu-like signs?
explanation: Spot on! The acute phase happens right after catching the virus, when the viral load shoots up and mild flu-like symptoms show up. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: An HIV-positive patient feels completely fine for eight years without taking meds. What stage is this?
explanation: You nailed it! Clinical latency is the long, quiet phase where the virus is active at low levels, but the patient usually feels healthy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: Why do clinics use the WHO staging system for HIV when lab tests for CD4 count are missing?

options.A: To guide clinical management using observable signs when CD4 counts are unavailable
options.B: To calculate the precise date when the patient was initially infected
options.C: To predict the exact genetic strain of the virus infecting the patient
options.D: To accurately measure the exact viral load circulating in the plasma

explanation: That's right! When lab equipment is scarce, checking physical signs and symptoms helps nurses and doctors choose the best care plan. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: Which health issue puts an HIV-positive patient into WHO Clinical Stage 4?

options.A: A normal CD4 count with no physical complaints
options.B: Kaposi sarcoma or severe opportunistic infections
options.C: Recurrent common colds and mild skin rashes
options.D: Persistent generalized swollen lymph nodes only

explanation: Spot on! Stage 4 involves severe illnesses and indicator conditions that mark advanced HIV disease (AIDS). [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: What CD4 count marks the official shift from HIV to AIDS?
explanation: You got it! When the immune system's CD4 count drops below 200 cells/mm³, the diagnosis is classified as AIDS. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why does a low CD4 count cause the whole immune system to fail?

options.A: CD4 cells seal the lymphatic vessels to trap invading bacteria
options.B: CD4 cells directly produce all the red blood cells in the body
options.C: CD4 cells act as master coordinators that activate other immune cells
options.D: CD4 cells form a physical barrier around organs to block viruses

explanation: Brilliant! CD4 helper cells are like the generals in an army—without them, the rest of the immune defenses don't know how to fight back. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: What do we call infections that take advantage of a weakened immune system?
explanation: Spot on! These are germs that a healthy immune system easily handles, but they 'seize the opportunity' when defenses are low. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)

question: Which cancer is linked to advanced HIV and caused by human herpesvirus 8?
explanation: You've got it! Kaposi sarcoma causes distinct purple or brown skin lesions and can affect internal organs in advanced HIV. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)
